findings: The ceiling strip lights flicker in step with the mains power. The phone camera picked this up clearly: a strong signal across about two-thirds of the 18 minutes. The audio hum was mostly drowned out by people talking, so it was not used.

I compared the flicker pattern with the national grid frequency record (Elexon, 15-second data) for 10:00–18:00 UTC on 8 Nov. It matched best at 11:42:39 UTC, with a score of 0.98 out of 1. The next-best time scored 0.84.
The stated start time of 13:42:37 is not among the strong matches.

Both halves of the video, checked separately, point to the same start time to within 1 second, so the result is consistent across the whole clip. The match also weakens quickly if the time is moved by 10 or 60 seconds, so it pins down one specific moment.
No time on the nearby days (5–11 Nov) matched as well. The best of those scored 0.84, so the recording was very likely made on 8 November.
I saw no sign that the clip was cut or joined. The two halves agree, which fits one continuous recording. Checks at this level of detail cannot fully rule out editing, though.
input.what_it_means: The date holds, but the time of day does not. The recording shows the room at about 11:42–12:01 UTC (UK local time), not 13:42–14:01. The gap is almost exactly 2 hours, which suggests a wrong time-zone or clock setting (such as a phone set to UTC+2) rather than random drift. It does not by itself show anyone acted deliberately. If the dispute depends on what happened in the room between about 13:42 and 14:01, this video does not show that period.
